directive: Valerius continues down the road. He keeps combat possible within the simulation while ordering his most trusted men to establish unity through parity and coordination: each commands a specialized section where he excels rather than being blindly concentrated against an enemy.

events.title: THE ROAD TIGHTENS INTO BROKEN GROUND
events.body: On 11 August, Valerius keeps the column on the road as its surface becomes rougher and the surrounding ground begins to break the clean visibility enjoyed on the previous marches. The road remains usable, but several bends and shallow rises make it possible for movement ahead to disappear from the main column for short periods. Valerius therefore keeps the hundred-man guard distributed instead of drawing it inward around the command group. The Vexillum Valerianum stays with the command element while mounted veterans maintain observation beyond the next rise and infantry veterans protect the spaces through which the main body must pass. No enemy is yet seen, but the changing ground gives the march a more serious character than the open stretches behind them. The expedition continues without stopping, treating the road itself as something to be watched rather than trusted blindly.

events.title: VALERIUS DIVIDES THE GUARD WITHOUT DIVIDING ITS UNITY
events.body: On 12 August, Valerius formally refines the guard's marching arrangement so that his most trusted men command specific sections according to their individual strengths rather than being gathered into one dense protective knot. Titus Varenus takes responsibility for a close infantry sector where disciplined shield work and short-range control are most valuable, while Lucius Atilius commands the opposite infantry sector and keeps its movement independent but synchronized. Gnaeus Fabius oversees the central infantry interval, preserving a passage through the formation so that men can move between sectors instead of becoming trapped in one mass. Other veterans take corresponding mounted, skirmishing, observation, and reserve sectors, with each specialist paired with men capable of supporting the same task from the neighboring sector. Signals and visual references from the Vexillum Valerianum allow the sectors to act with parity: none is abandoned to fight alone, but none waits passively for the others to collapse inward. Valerius makes the principle explicit that unity will come from coordination, mutual support, and equal responsibility rather than from clumping his best men together.

events.title: LOCAL TRACKS REVEAL WHO HAS BEEN USING THE ROAD
events.body: On 13 August, several travelers encountered along the road provide a different kind of warning when they describe seeing armed men farther ahead moving away from the settled fields. Their account is not treated as proof of an organized enemy force, but the direction and timing are recorded alongside the scouts' own observations. The road shows signs of recent traffic that are difficult to distinguish immediately from ordinary travelers, and Valerius orders the mounted screen to examine the approaches without breaking contact with the main body. The expedition learns that the road is being used by more people than its earlier agricultural contacts had suggested, including men who do not appear to be traveling for trade or farming. The information does not yet establish an enemy's strength or intention. By evening, however, the guard is prepared for the possibility that the next encounter will be hostile rather than merely another local contact.

events.title: ARMED MEN APPEAR AHEAD OF THE COLUMN
events.body: On 14 August, the forward screen reports armed men occupying a bend ahead where the road narrows between rising ground and rougher terrain. Valerius does not send Titus Varenus, Lucius Atilius, or the other trusted veterans charging blindly into the position; instead, he orders the guard's established sectors to hold their parity and reveal the hostile force's strength before committing the main body. The cavalry widens its observation while the infantry sectors maintain enough distance from one another to prevent a single attack from striking the entire guard at once. The armed group begins moving toward the column and looses a small number of missiles, making clear that the encounter is no longer merely suspicious movement on the road. Valerius keeps the command group behind the first defensive sectors and orders the road ahead denied without allowing the enemy to dictate the formation. The opposing men now have to deal with several mutually supporting Roman positions instead of one concentrated target. The road becomes a battlefield by circumstance, but Valerius has ensured that his most trusted men enter it as commanders of a coordinated system rather than as a single spearpoint.

events.title: THE GUARD HOLDS ITS SECTORS AND THE ROAD BECOMES A BATTLEFIELD
events.body:
On 15 August, the armed group commits to the attack, and you answer by keeping the guard spread across the sectors you established rather than allowing the road to compress your best men into a single knot. The first rush strikes the left side of the column, where Titus Varenus is already positioned with his close-fighting infantry, and the impact is hard enough to stagger the forward files. You can see the danger immediately: if the left is pulled inward to help itself, the whole formation will lose the intervals that make coordinated movement possible.

Titus holds his ground without freezing his men in place, giving a measured step and then another as the pressure rises. Lucius Atilius does the same on the opposite side, maintaining reach and refusing to let the attackers turn the road into one undifferentiated melee. Their sectors are separate in position but equal in responsibility, each watching its neighboring sector and preparing to support it without abandoning its own ground.

At the center, Gnaeus Fabius keeps the interval open exactly as you ordered. Men move through it in controlled numbers, reinforcing pressure points before they become breaks in the line, while the surviving files on either side continue to see and answer one another. What had looked on the previous day like a training principle becomes a living battlefield system, with distance itself acting as part of the guard's protection.

The attackers try to exploit the rough bends in the road, where a fold in the ground can hide movement for a few heartbeats. Your mounted veterans answer by widening their arc instead of charging straight forward, forcing the enemy to reveal more of its approach before committing its own strength. Gaius Valerius and Lucius Marcius maintain the moving screen, while other mounted guards watch the flanks for any attempt to slip around the infantry sectors.

The first exchange is dominated by missiles and short advances, and the sound of shields, wood, and iron becomes constant along the road. Publius Servilius and Numerius Cassius use their distance weapons from positions that remain tied to the infantry rather than drifting away from support. Their fire is not a separate battle; it is part of the same coordinated pattern, with each specialist creating an opening for another specialist to exploit.

You remain behind the first defensive sectors long enough to see where the enemy is actually committing itself. You do not throw Titus, Lucius, or the other trusted veterans forward blindly, and you do not sacrifice the formation simply to make the fight look more decisive. Instead, you wait until the lines have stabilized enough for your own participation to add strength rather than confusion.

When the moment comes, you advance into the fighting yourself. Your Roman panoply closes around you, your shield taking the blows that would otherwise reach the body behind it, while your gladius and double-reinforced pilum become the weapons you personally bring into the line rather than symbols carried at a distance. The oath embodied in the pilum is now visible in action: you are at the head of the battle, but you are there without abandoning command of the men who depend upon you.

The attackers then attempt a concentrated push against the road's narrowest point. Titus Varenus absorbs the immediate pressure while Lucius Atilius shifts enough of his sector to threaten the attacker's exposed side, and Gnaeus Fabius sends a controlled reinforcement through the center without closing the interval. No part of the guard fights alone, yet no part is crowded into the others.

For several minutes the battle becomes a sequence of local struggles rather than one single collision. A man driven backward on one side finds the neighboring sector already moving to cover the space, while another advances because the sector beside him has created room. The result is a strange battlefield rhythm in which the guard appears loose from a distance but becomes tightly coordinated whenever the enemy touches any individual part of it.

The attackers manage brief penetrations, and the fighting grows close enough for shield rims and sword points to decide moments at arm's length. You move where the pressure is highest, striking alongside your men rather than ordering them to endure what you would not endure yourself. Yet the command system remains intact: signals still travel, sector leaders still make decisions, and the Vexillum Valerianum remains a visible reference point behind the active line.

The enemy begins losing the ability to choose where the engagement happens. The mounted screen keeps its outer pressure, the infantry sectors deny the narrowest approaches, and the central interval allows your men to reinforce trouble without forming a vulnerable mass. Their attack becomes a series of increasingly isolated efforts, each one meeting a different Roman response tailored to the ground and the immediate danger.

Titus Varenus is forced to give ground for a short distance, but he does so deliberately rather than in rout, drawing the attackers into a position where Lucius Atilius can threaten their flank. Gnaeus Fabius immediately recognizes the change and moves the central support through the opening before the enemy can exploit it. The adjustment is quick enough that the attackers find the space they thought they had created suddenly covered from two directions.

You press forward with the renewed line. The fighting around you becomes confused for a moment as men from different sectors cross, separate, and reform, but the confusion belongs to movement rather than collapse. Your guard continues to behave as a network of specialized parts with a common purpose, proving the principle you established two days earlier under the one circumstance that cannot be imitated in training: real danger.

The hostile group finally begins to lose cohesion. Some men turn toward the rough ground beside the road, others hesitate when they realize that the Roman line is not breaking, and several are cut off from the forward thrust they had begun. Your men do not chase automatically, because you have not yet established what lies beyond the immediate ground and because an undisciplined pursuit would throw away the advantage your formation has just earned.

By the time the attackers withdraw beyond immediate contact, five of your men have suffered wounds serious enough to remove them temporarily from active duty, but none of your men is lost permanently. They remain part of your force and are moved safely into the column for treatment and recovery rather than being written out of the campaign. The battle has therefore imposed a real cost without turning a difficult engagement into an irreversible loss of your men.

When the fighting finally falls silent, you can see the road littered with broken equipment, spent missiles, disturbed earth, and the marks of bodies moving in every direction. Several attackers have failed to escape and are taken alive, while others disappear beyond the immediate field before your cavalry can close every exit. You order the ground secured and the wounded protected, not because the danger has vanished, but because the first duty after surviving the clash is to preserve the force that survived it.

The road remains under your control at the end of the engagement. More importantly, the hundred-man guard has now passed a genuine test of its defining doctrine: Titus Varenus, Lucius Atilius, Gnaeus Fabius, and the other specialists maintained distinct responsibilities, supported one another, and prevented the enemy from turning concentration against you. You leave the battlefield knowing that the arrangement is no longer merely an idea of yours or an exercise rehearsed in safety; it has been tested under actual weapons and has held.

classification_audit.qualification_basis: Extraordinary military engagement in which Valerius personally enters combat while the newly established distributed command doctrine is tested under actual attack.

events.title: THE CAPTIVES REVEAL THE ROAD HAS BEEN WATCHED
events.body: On 16 August, the expedition secures the immediate road section and tends the wounded before moving the column forward again. The five wounded are withdrawn from active duty and placed temporarily unavailable, while the rest of the guard remains distributed so that the column does not become defenseless simply because the fighting has ended. Several of the attackers who failed to escape are taken alive, and their equipment and statements are recorded without assuming that every member of the group belonged to a larger organization. The unexpected revelation is that the captives describe having watched this stretch of road before the attack, confirming that the danger was not simply a spontaneous clash but part of an existing pattern of observation whose wider extent remains unknown. Valerius orders no uncontrolled pursuit, and the cavalry instead watches the exits from the road while the infantry sectors maintain the ground already secured. Local travelers who had earlier warned the column are questioned again, allowing the expedition to compare their observations with what has now actually occurred. The result is a more reliable picture of the immediate danger, but not a complete explanation of who organized the attackers or how far their activity extends. The column therefore leaves the battlefield behind without pretending that the road has suddenly become completely safe.

events.title: VALERIUS CONTINUES THE MARCH WITH THE GUARD STILL DISTRIBUTED
events.body: On 17 August, Valerius orders the march to continue down the road with the guard still divided into its specialized sectors and the wounded kept safely within the column rather than exposed to another engagement. The Vexillum Valerianum remains with the command group, while the mounted screen moves ahead in staggered observation and the infantry sectors preserve deliberate intervals through which support can pass. Titus Varenus, Lucius Atilius, and Gnaeus Fabius retain their respective responsibilities, and the other veterans continue commanding the specific tasks for which their individual equipment and methods make them most useful. The recent fight has not caused Valerius to abandon the road, but it has changed the way the expedition treats every bend, rise, and side path beyond the immediate secured ground. No new land is claimed and no financial transaction is realized from the encounter. The expedition ends the week moving forward again, more informed about the dangers on the road and with its most trusted men proving their value through coordination rather than concentration.

personal_guard.command_structure: distributed specialist sectors with parity and mutual support

valerius_equipment.material_source: Valerius personal mines and estate stores
valerius_equipment.craftsmen: finest smiths of the estate and foundries
valerius_equipment.shield: new personal shield; exceptionally intricate and structurally tough; deliberately more intricate than Valerius's weapons as a symbol of devotion to protection and defense
valerius_equipment.gladius: personal high-quality Roman gladius; reputation linked to Valerius's established combat record
valerius_equipment.pilum: double-reinforced personal pilum; carries Valerius's oath to march at the head of every battle and personally participate
valerius_equipment.shield_piercing_record: individual truthful record for every confirmed shield personally pierced; no unverified encounter is added
valerius_equipment.kill_record: open truthful combat ledger; future confirmed individual kills may be recorded, but no unsupported kill count is asserted
